newsitem.title: UK: Work unaffected at Zaire copper/cobalt project.
newsitem.headline: Work unaffected at Zaire copper/cobalt project.

text.p: Development work at the giant Tenke Fengurume copper/cobalt property in southeastern Zaire was virtually unaffected by the fall of Lubumbashi, Tenke Mining Corp President Ted Webb said on Thursday.

"We have lost just three hours work in total, and that was welcoming the Alliance soldiers...there has been no looting, no pillaging, or threat to mine staff," Webb said at a presentation to the London-based Association of Mining Analysts (AMA).
"We don't see any delays or interruptions happening there," he said.

Company officials are in hourly contact with their mine staff in Zaire. The town of Kolwezi has also fallen to the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), who have asked state-owned mining firm Gecamines to carry on with their existing operations.
Earlier today that there were some 900 ADFL soldiers in Lubumbashi - the capital of Shaba - with the fighting having moved on to the airport, some 16 km to the south, officials said.
There has been heavy fighting there, but the airport is also expected to fall to the ADFL, either later on Thursday or on Friday morning.
The ADFL, led by Laurent Kabila, is seeking to overthrow Zaire's long-time President Mobutu Sese Seko. Kabila's forces have captured vast swathes of Zaire in the six-month rebellion.
Canada's Tenke Mining is developing a vast copper/cobalt mine in the mineral-rich Shaba provine of the troubled African country, signing a deal with Zaire's government last December.
The project, the first major foreign investment in Zaire since the 1970s, is a joint-venture with Gecamines who have a 45 percent holding.

Webb said that he and Tenke Board Chairman Adolf Lundin met with Kabila earlier this week. Both the rebels and the current Zaire government are aware that the World Bank and the IMF are monitoring Tenke-Fengurume as a barometer for future foreign investment.
"He (Kabila) supported the project, but will discuss arrangements. We have a fair degree of comfort with that," Webb said.

The ADFL seems to be a body of people who want Zaire's economy to go forward, and privatisation is on its agenda with a pent-up expectation of better things taking place in the country, as is the case in South Africa, Webb added.
"We are having dialogue with all factions and will continue to do so," he said.
The mine is projected to start producing 100,000 tonnes of copper a year by mid-2000 and 8,000 tonnes of cobalt, eventually expanding to 400,000 tonnes a year of copper.
